extracted.intended_audience: communication scholars, journalism researchers, and content analysts studying/operationalizing hard vs soft news
extracted.subtask_description: Provide standardized, multi-dimensional conceptualization and content-analysis operationalizations for distinguishing 'hard' and 'soft' news items (topic, focus, style) and guidance for measurement and coding practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension: Topic/Events (topic dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dimension referring to the subject matter of the news item (e.g. politics, economy, sports, culture). Most studies use the main topics of an item as an indicator for hard vs soft news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common practice: treat foreign and domestic politics, economy and finance as 'hard' topics; sports, celebrities, royal families, crime, scandals and service often coded as 'soft' (De Swert, 2007). Caveat: topics are proxy indicators — the same topic can be framed differently (e.g., crime can be hard if linked to policy or soft if focused on perpetrators/victims). Studies differ on coding single vs multiple topics per item. Use topic coding only alongside focus and style to avoid misleading classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension: News production (production characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the journalistic production process used in some definitions: timeliness, urgency, scheduling (e.g., breaking/urgent events vs nonscheduled stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many authors treat timeliness/urgency as a key indicator (e.g., Shoemaker & Cohen: hard = timely/urgent; soft = nonscheduled). The article recommends caution: production features are not intrinsic content characteristics, are hard to infer reliably from content alone, and therefore are often excluded from content-analytic operationalizations. Where production traits are used, supplement content analysis with newsroom surveys/observations to measure them reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension: News focus (focus dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which aspects of a topic/event are emphasized — e.g., linkage to the public good vs individual-level consequences; thematic (contextualized) vs episodic (case-based) framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include whether a story contextualizes an event with policy implications (hard) or concentrates on the individual/incident and personal details (soft). The focus dimension should be coded separately from topic because framing determines linkage to public affairs. Recommended focus sub-codings are Individual–Societal relevance and Episodic–Thematic framing (see explicit coding schemes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension: News style (style dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the story is presented — e.g., factual/text-oriented vs personalized/visually oriented; presence of journalist's voice; emotionalization, sensationalism, informal vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two sub-dimensions commonly operationalized: (a) appearance of journalists' subjective impressions/point of view (analysis/feature/commentary vs detached factual reporting), and (b) story ambiance/sensational presentation (dramatisation, affective wording, visuals). Style indicators are suitable for content analysis and are important for capturing 'softening' below agenda level. Code style separately from topic and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension: News reception/effects (reception dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience- and effect-related characteristics referenced in some definitions: whether news is entertaining, personally useful, or politically important; differential audience interest patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reception/effect criteria (e.g., perceived importance, entertainment value, gendered interest differences) are conceptually relevant but not direct content attributes. To include reception perspectives, combine content analysis with surveys or effects studies. The article notes many studies mention reception but few measure it directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed standardized definition principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'harder' and 'softer' forms of news with respect to message elements that potentially have an impact on perceptions of public affairs; focus on content characteristics measurable in news messages rather than production/timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications: exclude timeliness as a primary content-coded indicator (timeliness is not a content characteristic and its relation to political perceptions is unclear). Focus measurement on topic, focus and style dimensions in combination. Use multi-dimensional instruments and avoid simple uni-dimensional/topic-only classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization: Topic dimension — Political relevance (four binary aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding whether a news item deals with norms, goals, interests and activities related to authoritative, generally binding decisions about societal issues. Four aspects indicate political relevance: (1) societal actors in disagreement, (2) decision-making authorities involved, (3) presence of a planned or realized decision/measure/program, (4) persons/groups concerned by the decision/measure/program. For each aspect presence =1 / non-presence =0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code each of the four aspects separately as 0/1 and use the combined score as the item's political relevance indicator. Examples and precise inclusion rules are provided in the appendix; this operationalization is intended to capture political/public-affairs relevance rather than topical labels alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization: Focus dimension — Individual vs Societal relevance (0/1/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether a news item stresses personal/private meaning/consequences (individual) or general/overall consequences for society (societal). 0 = pure/predominant individual focus; 1 = mixed; 2 = pure/predominant societal focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose middle category if attention to both aspects is about equal. Examples: climate-change story that stresses higher bills = individual; stresses systemic changes = societal. Use alongside political relevance coding to capture linkage to public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization: Focus dimension — Episodic vs Thematic framing (0/1/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether the item presents an issue via a specific example/event/case (episodic) or places it in broader context with figures, commentary and links to causes/implications (thematic). 0 = episodic; 1 = mixed; 2 = thematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unemployment story about one person's plight = episodic; unemployment story presenting statistics and policy commentary = thematic. Middle category if both are equally present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization: Style dimension — Personal vs Impersonal reporting (0/1/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether a news item includes explicit statements of the reporting journalists' personal impressions, interpretations, or opinions. 0 = purely/predominantly personal; 1 = mix; 2 = purely/predominantly impersonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count quotes from other actors (experts, politicians) as journalists' personal voice. Choose middle category if both personal and impersonal elements are mixed. Use this to identify feature/analysis/commentary vs detached reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization: Style dimension — Emotional vs Unemotional reporting (0/1/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether the presentation uses verbal, visual or audio means that potentially arouse or amplify emotions (emotional) versus matter-of-fact presentation (unemotional). 0 = purely/predominantly emotional; 1 = mix; 2 = purely/predominantly unemotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional indicators include dramatization (presenting events as exceptional/thrilling), affective wording/superlatives, use of present tense for past events, pronounced accentuation, reporting or visually presenting explicit expressions of emotion. Note: this category refers to presentation techniques, not the inherent emotion-arousing potential of the topic itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Multi-dimensional measurement and cluster analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat hard vs soft as a strict dichotomy; instead analyse dimensions in combination (topic, focus, style) and use approaches such as cluster analysis to construct clusters of news items representing varying combinations of dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: yields nuanced, fine-grained analyses; allows combining content analysis with audience/effect studies; captures changes below the news-agenda level (e.g., style shifts). The authors recommend using commonly shared concepts and operationalizations to increase comparability and cumulativity across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on common measurement pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Cautions drawn from the literature: many studies omit operationalization details; production- and effects-related characteristics are difficult to infer reliably from content; topic-only classifications are misleading; crime/topic categories can be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve reliability and validity: (a) make operationalizations explicit, (b) code topic, focus and style separately, (c) supplement content analysis with surveys/observations when measuring production or reception variables, and (d) report intercoder reliability. Be wary of pre-assigning topics to hard/soft without considering framing and style.
